Is it a good or bad thing when a bank sells your mortgage to another bank or company? Should the consumer be concerned about this? I'm a first time home buyer in the US and I've been shopping around for competitive mortgage interest rates. I have noticed that at least one of the banks offering a mortgage will sell my mortgage to another bank.
Question about banks re-selling your mortgage
The terms stay the same, and they're required to notify you of the change in mortgage holder and where to send your mortgage payment. Imo no big deal.
Thanks for getting back to me. This makes sense.

It doesn't necessarily mean anything good or bad.

A lot of lenders sell 100% of the paper they write as soon as the loan closes. They sell if for more than the amount that they loaned you, but less than the amount you will eventually pay over 30 years with interest, and make a profit.

Now, if you stop paying for a few months and your mortgage gets sold to a collections-type company, then that's bad.
Thanks for the heads up. Don't plan to miss a mortgage payment but hey, who does

The biggest difference I know of is that lenders who sell your mortgage often require much stricter terms. This isn't an issue if you have a decent downpayment and your income and assets are fairly straightforward. If you have more a more complex income situation then you may be better off going with a lender who will keep your mortgage on the books (although you may have to pay a slightly higher interest rate).

[WP] In death, every man is reduced to a book in a sacred, hidden library somewhere on Earth. Today an explorer finds the repository.

Library Of Man by Larry Heyl

My com buzzed. "There's been a breakthrough down at the lab. Come at once. Our subject is dying".

Fortunately I was on my way already. In less than a minute I flew through the door. My assistants were attaching electrodes to the subjects temples. He was 117 years old, his life force diminishing by the minute. We weren't killing him. He was just dying. It happens to all of us.

Everthing was ready and we were waiting, drinking coffee. Then he flatlined. There was nothing for us to do except monitor our equipment. The recorder kicked in. Everything seemed to be working. Within minutes it was over. He was gone.

"Now for the test", I said. My assistants hit the play button. In a darkened corner the hologram started. Everything was fuzzy. "Fast forward a few years", I said.

It looked like a birthday party. Kids were sitting around the table with a birthday cake on it candles ablaze. The cake got big and the candles were extinguished. One of my assistants said, "I hope he made a wish".

Fast forward again and we saw a soldering iron touching a circuit board. I said, "That must be his workshop where he modernized our com units.

"Bring us up to yesterday", I said. We saw feet on a gurney being wheeled through a door. It was eerie seeing the lab appear. The very room we were standing in was duplicated by a hologram and we were looking at it.

"It worked". We cheered. Time for some champagne.

At the time of his death his life flashed before him in a second. And we just recorded it. All of it. Now we can start building the library of man.

Currently testing out a bunch. Installed Ubuntu alongside Windows 8, after taking a two-year Linux hiatus (was previously using Arch with AwesomeWM, but got tired of it). Here's my experience so far:

  • Unity – nice-looking but not customizable. Don't miss drop-down application menus at all. Works well out of the box.

  • Gnome Shell – very similar to Unity, except for different behavior on the top panel. Global menubar replaced with menu buttons in the window decorations, but only for the small set of supported apps. Notifications are hidden on a bottom bar, which I don't like. Very customizable with shell extensions, but overall it's less polished than Unity.

  • Cinnamon – very good throwback interface for veteran users. I used this for a while before deciding to see what Gnome Shell was all about. Overall it's a great WM, but eventually I decided to embrace the future rather than cling to the past.

  • XFCE – great lightweight alternative to those listed above. I would definitely recommend for lower-spec systems. I didn't stick with it only because my system is powerful enough to make the eyecandy of other DEs worth it.

  • KDE Plasma – tried using it for a day, but it was just far too slow. Took 10+ seconds after logging in to display the desktop. Once it was displayed, things were still lagging and my cursor was jumping around randomly. My build isn't exactly high-end, but with an A10 and 8 GB of RAM that's not acceptable

So far I've decided to stick with Unity because it works and my distro was built around it. I'm probably going to try LxQt, which I just found out from this thread.

Edit: of course this is my opinion of DEs running on my machine. YMMV.
